title: Opinion: In political footwear, Mark Carney is the gentleman usher of the black-shod
html:
We keep trying to see the big political picture, the grand historical arc of where we have been, are and will be. The urge is especially understandable these days, with an erratic American President breathing all over us (even if he does get hemmed in by his midterm reversals).

The problem with the big picture, alas, is that you can never grasp it in total in the present, at the time you need to see it, because you are in it, wallowing and flailing and struggling to stay above the surface before the current has become clear. We cling in the meantime to half-formed warnings, but they only entangle us in the slippery reeds of anxiety.

Why not dive deep for a moment on a single alleged fact instead? How about the oft-reported detail that Mark Carney, our elbows-up-and-then-back-down Prime Minister, dislikes brown shoes and insists that men in the Prime Minister’s Office wear formal, black lace-up oxfords – serious bankerwear for a serious team at a serious time?

The rule has been in place since the beginning of Mr. Carney’s reign, and long before the Minister of Finance wore a pair of new black shoes to deliver last week’s budget. That’s mere tradition. Mr. Carney’s black-shoe decree is a way of life, with a long and well-heeled pedigree.

True, it’s a little anal, but so is the master-of-the-universe world of finance from which Mr. Carney hails (Goldman Sachs, the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, Brookfield), where one’s performance must always be on time and tickety-boo.

The real point of insisting on de rigueur black lace-up kicks? It lends the Carney brand a sober mien in the face of dire challenges to Canada’s economic health and sovereignty. The black shoes are a stabilizing counterweight to Mr. Carney’s reputation for policy flip-flops (in favour of the United States war on Iran, then against it; a champion of combatting climate change, but keen on pipelines; praising Donald Trump’s “peace” efforts in Ukraine, but opposing the U.S. purchase of Russian oil that Canada could have supplied; etc.).

At least we know he wants to be taken seriously, because he wants everyone on his team to wear serious black shoes. Canada has always felt threatened by the mob to our south. And so the Prime Minister is calling to the sole of our nation.

Black shoes are the opposite of the footwear preferred by Mr. Carney’s more progressive, left-leaning predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

Mr. Trudeau single-handedly established a newly transgressive fashion template in international politics by upending its stodgy fashion norms. His advanced-class footwear (brown? In town? With navy blue? How daring!) proclaimed his edgy progressive politics (eventually too progressive or too economically regressive to stay prime minister).

Mere weeks into Mr. Trudeau’s first appearance on the world stage in a navy-blue suit bottomed off with brown shoes, every executive, pol and journalist in the country was trying out the combo. (The Chewbacca Star Wars socks came later, at the Bloomberg Global Business Forum.)

The Bata Shoe Museum has a pair of Pierre Trudeau's brown leather sandals. His son, Justin, would favour dress shoes of this colour during his own career in politics.Duane Cole/The Globe and Mail

Whether Justin Trudeau wore brown shoes or black, he would sometimes add colourful socks. The Star Wars-themed ones are from a 2017 meeting with the Irish Taoiseach.Christinne Muschi and Yves Herman/Reuters

For his final Throne Speech in 2025, delivered by the King, Mr. Trudeau wore Adidas running shoes that stood out on the Senate carpet.Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press

Political leaders have this power. John F. Kennedy killed the fedora by not wearing a hat at his inauguration. Ronald Reagan popularized the brown suit (he thought they made him stand out in group photographs). Brian Mulroney brought back the double-breasted version. The establishment likes to play Follow the Leader.

And there is something to be said for it. Adrienne Clarkson, the former governor-general of Canada, notes in a memoir how appalled she was by the lack of formality in Paul Martin’s PMO. Jean Chrétien’s was more punctilious: People stood up whenever the p’tit gars prime minister entered the room. It was a rule. It was not the rule in former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne’s office, much to the astonishment of some of her federal colleagues.

Displays of respect can be taken too far, of course, even fetishized: See the abject suckholing of Marco Rubio and other members of Mr. Trump’s cabinet, who actually wore pairs of black Florsheim shoes the President gave them.

On the other hand, conformity can convey solidarity. A friend of mine, a former partner in the Boston Consulting Group, was once in charge of maintaining sartorial discipline in the company’s head office. The dress code included black lace-up shoes; black, blue or grey suits; and modest skirts. Blazers, sports jackets, grey flannels and especially brown shoes were absolutely verboten.

He understands how strict that rule seems these days, now that tech culture, working from home and casual Fridays have flattened our standards of formality.

But he still thinks the uniform of suits and black shoes made everyone more attentive to detail, and better team players. It suggested that everyone was on the ball and paying attention. It said: No one in this office is relaxed.

The business classes of many cultures favour shiny black shoes. At Tokyo's Hie shrine, someone has left a pair alongside wooden Japanese zori during a kendo competition.Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press

The shibboleth against brown shoes in the halls of power may be less universally observed than it once was, but it’s still going strong.

Larry Rosen, the chief executive officer of Harry Rosen, the men’s clothing store, claims the majority of dress shoes he sells are black. (Mr. Rosen himself prefers brown shoes, even with a blue suit – “they’re more European” – but nevertheless approves of the Prime Minister’s black-shoe rule for a team that has the serious job of running the world’s 10th-largest economy.)

Canadian lawyers are still pressured to wear well-shined black shoes when they appear in court.

It’s not a written rule, Paul Cochrane, a lawyer of more than four decades, told me recently, “but certainly within the profession, when appearing in gowns, black shoes are mandatory.” Why? Because judges sometimes claim they can’t “hear” counsel who are not wearing black shoes (that is, not showing sufficient respect for the bench).

Mr. Cochrane admits standards have fallen as the number of unrepresented and self-represented supplicants in court has risen.

“I attended an interim hearing in Hamilton Superior family court a few years ago,” he told me, “where a lawyer attended court in sandals and – I’m still so astonished that I find it hard to type – a mesh shirt. I was speechless.”

Luigi Mangione wore brown shoes to this New York court hearing in May, months before he pleaded guilty in the fatal shooting of a health-insurance executive.Steven Hirsch/Getty Images

But Mr. Carney’s preference for highly polished black lace-up oxfords has created a stir in the ranks of rank-and-file male office workers as well. The transition back to black from Trudeauvian brown has been anything but a slip-on for the common man.

For instance, here is Mr. Symbol, as we shall call him. He is a real person: mid-40s, socially liberal but politically independent, a father and a husband. He lives and works in downtown Toronto.

His style is tightly curated to evince an uncurated look: Think turned-up jeans with plaid sports jackets, the occasional waistcoat, mustard-coloured brogues, rusty Doc Martens, the odd surprising flouncy shirt thrown in for ironic flair.

The key to the look is its Barthesian unpredictability. It’s not foppish, but it can be fancy or footloose. You just can’t know ahead of time what’s coming, the way you could with men’s clothes for several centuries. In millennial fashion, disruption rules.

But to his own oppositional astonishment, Mr. Symbol recently caved to the national podia-geist and bought a pair of black lace-up shoes. It was traumatic, he recalled of his two-week-long decision-making process. He’s not a black-shoe type by nature, but he has a public-facing job that brings him into contact with business executives and the odd politician, and he felt the generalized public heat of our leader’s preference.

Mr. Symbol eventually settled on a pair of black lace-up bluchers, albeit with a contrasting brown sole – “a small token of my resistance” was how he described it. They cost a small fortune.

The clash between black and brown shoes is not new, of course. To discover more precisely what Mr. Carney’s black toecaps connote, a little shoe history is in order.

Human beings have been wearing shoe-like garments for at least 50,000 years, but the oldest surviving pair dates back only 5½ millenniums. They look a bit like Yeezy’s Adidas Foam Runners, and a lot more like opanke, basic doltish peasant garb. Grass was probably stuffed inside them as an insulator.

But in the 14th and 15th centuries, upper-class European footwear gets especially fancy and status-obsessed. (By then, Edward I has declared that three barleycorns equal an inch, which in turn standardizes shoe sizing.) During the reign of Edward III, the most desirable shoes get pointier and pointier: Some winklepicker toes are 18 inches (54 barleycorns) long. They are known as crakows (the style originated in what is now Poland) or poulaines, and are absurdly impractical – so long and elfin that their wearers develop bunions and/or fall on their faces, a lot.

Imagining Edward III's coronation nearly six centuries later, this artist gave the king period-appropriate pointy shoes.Illustrated London News, 1902

But courtiers wear them anyway because they convey wealth and aristocratic status: Anyone wearing a crakow doesn’t do manual work and is a person of leisure. They eventually become associated with sodomy and devil worship, because you can’t wear super-pointies and pray at the same time. Our choice of and enslavement to fashionable footwear, in other words, is as irrational in that era as it is today.

Edward III decrees that in England no shoe’s toe can be longer than two inches. (Royal footwear orders long predate Mr. Carney’s dictum.) This in turn produces the round- and square-toed pump, duck-billed footgear of rich material and colour, the status of whose wearer is now signalled in part by the height of their heels.

None of these fancy shoes are black or brown: In Hyacinthe Rigaud’s 1701 portrait of Louis XIV as the pinnacle of style, he’s wearing white pumps with a reddish heel, another signifier of royal status. Louis is 5 foot 4 and wears five-inch heels because that is what fashionable men do. The shoe has become one measure of the man.

From shoes to silk coats, Louis XIV set trends for French aristocrats that kept them competing for status at Versailles, and ideally in debt and less of a political threat.Portrait by Hyacinth Rigaud, 1701

In the late 1600s, everything changes, thanks to a little adventure known as the Enlightenment. Science begins to supplant religion. Philosophers pronounce and defend the rights of individuals. Encyclopedias are published; trade and capitalism flourish; the seeds of a yearning merchant class are sown. These trends eventually foment the French and American revolutions and their democracies – government based on the radical idea that all men are equal.

But the equality of men creates a problem for the elites and the upper classes, who want to hang on to their privilege and power in a populist era. A life of leisure based on inherited wealth is not something you want to advertise. So a new ideal of masculinity emerges: the self-sufficient man of action. And a life of action requires a new kind of shoe.

“In the 18th century in England and then on the continent,” Elizabeth Semmelhack, the director and senior curator of Toronto’s Bata Shoe Museum, explained to me recently, “boots become the new signifier of upper-class masculinity” – in part because riding boots imply that you are rich enough to own a horse, and therefore land.

The first Duke of Wellington, at left with Lord Nelson, left his name on a style of boot that caught on among British soldiers during the Napoleonic Wars.Mezzotint by S.W. Reynolds after J.P. Knight, ca. 1839, via Wellcome Collection

This is where the snobby distinction between black and brown shoes is born.

“The majority of working-class footwear in the 18th and 19th centuries was brown,” Ms. Semmelhack pointed out. “Labouring men who were in the city would have all been in dull, brown shoes.” How, then, can the upper classes nod to the working class – to the idea that all men are created equal – without joining their ranks and abandoning their elite status?

By using fashion to make new and subtler distinctions. “The idea that men are active goes against eons of belief that the upper class should never work,” Ms. Semmelhack said. “But its members need to express that they are men of action in a new way. And so the idea that you’ve gone to your estate, like the casual wearing of riding boots, becomes a part of British male attire.

“Boots suggest you’ve been out managing your land – maybe not really working, but doing active things, like hunting. So in the country, in the estate scenario, men are allowed to wear tweed, clothes that show that they’ve been outside and active.” That includes brown shoes, because “brown is a colour that hides dirt.”

Brown shoes become fashionable for aristocrats in the country (and for all those who wish to emulate them). In the city, the gentryman has a different problem. London’s bricklayers and plumbers and factory workers all wear brown shoes, and their masculinity and status as men of action are not in question.

“So how do you define the class difference in that scenario?” Ms. Semmelhack asked. “One way is in how you dress. So within the urban environment, very shiny, very clean black shoes become appropriate for upper-class activities, eventually making their way into jobs. Those jobs tend to be linked to things that are high level – finance, law, jobs like that.”

A journalist or a professor or an ad man can get away with suede brogues, but only because those professions occupy lower rungs of the social hierarchy. Power talks, and power walks, and when it does, it has to wear shiny black shoes.

Shoe-shining, while not as prolific as it was in the 19th and 20th centuries, is still a living business today.Duane Cole/The Globe and Mail

…
summary: The Prime Minister has revived the sartorial shibboleth against brown. The edict is more revealing than it seems
